entities.name: Social Democratic Party of Germany
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD), founded in 1863 as the General German Workers' Association, is one of the world's oldest and most influential political parties — the party that created German trade unionism, the welfare state, the 8-hour working day, and women's suffrage in Germany, while being persecuted by Bismarck, banned by Hitler, and reborn as the governing party of West Germany and reunified Germany. The SPD's history encompasses the entire arc of German modernity from Wilhelmine industrialism to 21st-century coalition government.

Ferdinand Lassalle founded the General German Workers' Association in 1863; August Bebel and Wilhelm Liebknecht merged it with the Social Democratic Workers' Party to create the SPD in 1875. Bismarck's Anti-Socialist Laws (1878-1890) banned the party but failed to destroy it — the SPD emerged stronger and in 1912 became the largest party in the Reichstag. The SPD's 1914 vote for war credits — supporting Kaiser Wilhelm's entry into WWI — was the most contested decision in socialist history, splitting international socialism.

Kurt Schumacher rebuilt the SPD after Hitler's dissolution of all parties in 1933. Willy Brandt's Ostpolitik (1969-1974) — normalized relations with East Germany and Soviet bloc — was the most significant foreign policy achievement of any postwar German chancellor. Gerhard Schröder's 2002-2005 Agenda 2010 labor market reforms ('Hartz reforms') were the most painful but economically transformative policy in post-war German history. Olaf Scholz became SPD chancellor in 2021 leading a three-party coalition.
